title: Two monsters
summary_es: Crítica comparada de *Frankenstein* y *Drácula*: dos miedos opuestos —lo que fabricamos y lo que viene de fuera— y cómo hemos suavizado los dos.
prediction_prompt: What do you picture when you hear "Frankenstein" and "Dracula"? Where do those pictures come from: the books or the films?

sentences.text: Ask almost anyone to describe Frankenstein and they will give you a flat-topped giant with bolts in his neck who walks as though wading through wet cement and communicates in groans.
Ask them about Dracula and you will get a cape, an accent and a fondness for dramatic entrances.
Both portraits are the work of the cinema, and both are, as it happens, close to the opposite of what the novelists wrote.
That would be a mere curiosity if the mistakes were random.
They are not.
In each case we have quietly rewritten the monster into something easier to live with.
Take the older book first.
Mary Shelley's novel, published in 1818 and begun when she was eighteen, contains no bolts, no laboratory assistant and very little lumbering.
Her creature is agile, fast and, above all, articulate.
He teaches himself to speak, and then to read, by eavesdropping on a family of cottagers, and his education is completed by a bundle of lost books that happens to include Paradise Lost.
When he finally confronts the man who made him, he does not growl.
He argues, at length and rather better than his maker, that he was born harmless and has been made vicious by neglect.
That is the heart of the book, and it is exactly what the popular version removes.
The scientist, Victor Frankenstein, is not punished for the arrogance of creating life; the novel is curiously uninterested in how he does it and disposes of the matter in a few evasive sentences.
His real offence comes a moment later, when he looks at what he has made, finds it ugly, and runs away.
Everything that follows, every death in a story with a great many of them, flows from that single refusal.
Shelley's subject is not forbidden knowledge.
It is abandonment.
It is telling that we have transferred the maker's name to the thing he made, since the creature in the novel is never given one.
To be nameless is to belong to nobody.
The dumb, staggering monster of the screen is a comfort by comparison: he cannot reproach us, because he cannot speak.
Give him back his voice and the tale ceases to be about a danger that escaped and becomes one about a child that was disowned.
It is a far less convenient story, and it has not dated in the slightest.
Bram Stoker's Dracula, which appeared in 1897, has been softened in a different way.
A century of adaptation has turned the Count into a seducer, melancholy, well dressed, more to be pitied than feared.
The novel offers little support for this.
Its vampire is, when we first meet him, an old man with hair on his palms and breath that turns the stomach, and after the opening chapters he is scarcely on the page at all.
He has very few lines.
He is glimpsed at windows, suspected in fogs, inferred from the condition of his victims.
What fills the space he leaves is paperwork.
The book is assembled entirely from documents: diaries, letters, telegrams, a ship's log, newspaper cuttings, even a doctor's notes spoken into a phonograph.
Its heroes do not defeat their enemy by courage alone.
They defeat him by filing.
They collate their records, type them up in order, compare dates, consult railway timetables and track him across Europe like a missing parcel.
Against a creature who has been alive for centuries, Stoker sets the full machinery of the modern office, and the office wins.
The contrast with Shelley could hardly be sharper.
Her monster comes from inside: from a laboratory, from a family, from the best intentions of a gifted young man.
His comes from outside, by sea, from a far corner of the continent, bringing with him boxes of his native earth.
Hers begs for a place at the fireside and is driven off.
His acquires a house near London through a perfectly respectable solicitor and has to be hunted out of it.
One novel worries about what we owe to the things we make.
The other worries about what might be done to us by something that owes us nothing.
They differ, too, in what they ask of the reader.
Dracula is, for all its horrors, a reassuring book.
The threat is foreign, the defenders are decent, and by the last page order has been restored and the papers have been put away.
Frankenstein offers no such tidying.
It ends on the ice, with the maker dead, the creature mourning him and promising to destroy himself, and nobody in a position to say which of them was the monster.
Stoker closes the file.
Shelley leaves it open on the desk.
It is tempting to conclude that Shelley's is the greater novel, and on most days I would agree.
But the comparison is less a ranking than a diagnosis, because the two books describe the two ways in which we have always preferred to be frightened.
We can fear the stranger at the gate, or we can fear our own handiwork.
The first is the more popular, for the simple reason that it flatters us: it draws a line with ourselves on the right side of it.
The second draws no line at all.
Every new anxiety seems to get sorted, sooner or later, into one tradition or the other.
Diseases are discussed in the language of Stoker: they arrive, they cross borders, they are to be kept out.

Our cleverest machines are discussed, increasingly, in the language of Shelley, and it is striking how often the conversation drifts towards whether they might turn on us, as though the creature's violence, and not his maker's flight, were the point of the story.
We are still reaching for the version with the bolts.
The book, patient as ever, is still asking what we intend to do about the thing once it opens its eyes.

language_focus.explanation_es: La comparación avanza por parejas de frases construidas igual: *Hers begs… His acquires…*, *One novel worries… The other worries…*, *Stoker closes the file. Shelley leaves it open on the desk.* La simetría hace el contraste sin necesidad de explicarlo.
*They defeat him by filing*, *like a missing parcel*, *and the office wins*: rebajar lo heroico a lo administrativo es una forma muy británica de hacer crítica con humor sin dejar de hablar en serio.

tasks.prompt: What is the essay's main argument?

options.text: Film versions of classic novels are always inferior to the original books
The two novels embody opposite fears, and we soften both

tasks.rationale_es: Un monstruo viene de dentro y otro de fuera; a los dos los hemos reescrito para que incomoden menos.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 3, 6, 8 and 10 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.

headings.text: One file closed, one left open

tasks.rationale_es: El párrafo 3 trata de la verdadera culpa de Victor; el 6, del papeleo que vence al vampiro; el 8, de los dos finales; el 10, de las angustias de hoy.

tasks.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how does the creature in the novel differ from the screen monster?

options.text: He is considerably larger and far more violent than in the films

tasks.rationale_es: En la novela es ágil, rápido y, sobre todo, habla muy bien.

tasks.prompt: What, for the writer, is Victor Frankenstein's true fault?

options.text: Lying to his family about his experiments for many years

tasks.rationale_es: No es crear vida, sino mirar lo creado, encontrarlo feo y huir.

tasks.prompt: The novel explains in detail how the creature is brought to life.
tasks.rationale_es: Lo despacha en unas pocas frases evasivas.

tasks.prompt: Why is the speechless screen monster "a comfort"?

options.text: He is less physically dangerous than the creature in the book

tasks.rationale_es: Si no habla, no puede reprocharnos nada.

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 4, "it has not dated in the slightest" means the story…

options.text: was published without a date on its original title page

tasks.rationale_es: *To date* = quedar anticuado. No ha envejecido nada.

tasks.prompt: How has a century of adaptation changed Dracula?

options.text: It has made him more talkative and more frightening than before
It has made him a romantic figure

tasks.rationale_es: Lo ha convertido en un seductor melancólico y bien vestido.

tasks.prompt: What does the writer mean by "They defeat him by filing"?

options.text: They report him to the police
They sharpen their weapons carefully before the final fight

tasks.rationale_es: Ganan ordenando documentos, comparando fechas y consultando horarios.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer compare the pursuit to tracking "a missing parcel"?

options.text: To show the heroes are careless
To suggest that the Count was unusually small and light to carry
To make the heroic chase sound comically bureaucratic

tasks.rationale_es: Rebaja la persecución heroica a un trámite de oficina: es el tono irónico del ensayo.

tasks.prompt: In the writer's reading, both monsters come from outside the society they threaten.
tasks.rationale_es: El de Shelley nace dentro: de un laboratorio, de una familia.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer call Dracula "a reassuring book"?

options.text: Evil is external and is finally defeated
It is written in simple, comforting language for younger readers

tasks.rationale_es: La amenaza viene de fuera, los defensores son buenos y al final se restablece el orden.

tasks.prompt: According to the writer, why is fear of "the stranger at the gate" more popular?

options.text: It is much older than any other fear known to human beings
It lets us see ourselves as innocent

tasks.rationale_es: Nos halaga: traza una línea y nos deja en el lado bueno.

tasks.prompt: The writer has seen every film adaptation of both novels.
tasks.rationale_es: Habla de un siglo de adaptaciones, pero no dice cuántas ha visto.

tasks.prompt: What does the final sentence imply about the debate over intelligent machines?

options.text: That we focus on the danger and overlook our own responsibility
That such machines will certainly turn, one day, on the very people who made them

tasks.rationale_es: Seguimos mirando la violencia de la criatura y no la huida de quien la hizo.
